passage: The first time I voted, last spring, I almost didn't go. The queue at the school booth near our flat was long, the sun was harsh, and I had an internship report due. But Dadaji had asked me the week before, "Vishal, will you take me?" His knees are bad and he doesn't trust auto drivers anymore. So I went. We stood in line together, him leaning on my arm and telling me about his first election, decades ago. When the officer inked my finger, I felt oddly grown up. Afterwards, my friend Thomas and I spent the evening filling out forms for Dadaji's pension renewal. It took three hours. Looking back, it wasn't a big dramatic day. But it was the first time I felt like a real citizen and a real grandson.

qa.q: Where was the polling booth?
qa.a: At the school near Vishal's flat.

qa.q: What did Vishal feel when the officer inked his finger?
qa.a: He felt oddly grown up, like a real citizen, as if he had stepped into adult responsibility.

qa.q: Why was it wise of Vishal to go despite the long queue and his report?
qa.a: Voting and helping his grandfather were duties that mattered more than a short delay, and they strengthened his family bond.

qa.q: How might Dadaji have experienced the day?
qa.a: He probably felt cared for and proud, sharing memories of his own first election with his grandson. 🙂

grounding: A young man looks back on his first vote and helping his grandfather, joining civic duty and filial care.

Note from Vidya, volunteer coordinator at the ward welfare office.

Suraj, twenty, has volunteered with us on Saturdays since January. He first came to help register voters in the ward's slum pockets. He was shy at first, but by March he was walking door to door on his own, explaining the forms patiently to elderly residents.

In April he missed two Saturdays. When he came back, he told me quietly that his aunt, who raised him, had been unwell and he had been taking her to appointments. He did not want to let us down, so he asked if he could do paperwork from home those weeks.

He has now started a small team of college friends for the health camp next month.

Next step: I will recommend him for the district youth award. — Vidya

qa.q: What did Suraj first come to help with?
qa.a: Registering voters in the ward's slum pockets.

qa.q: What does Suraj asking to do paperwork from home show about his feelings?
qa.a: He felt responsible both to his aunt and to the volunteer work, and didn't want to let either down.

qa.q: How could the welfare office support young volunteers like Suraj?
qa.a: By offering flexible tasks when family needs arise, as Vidya did, so they can keep contributing without guilt.

qa.q: How might Suraj's aunt feel about him?
qa.a: She would likely feel cared for and proud of the young man she raised, as he balances caring for her with helping others.

grounding: A coordinator records a young man balancing civic volunteering with caring for the relative who raised him.

passage:
Thursday night.

Filed my first income tax return today! Got a little stipend income from the internship, and Papa said it's time I learnt. Mehak sat with me on the video call because she did hers last year. Took two hours, lots of confusion, one small panic about a missing form. But done. Felt weirdly proud pressing submit.

Then went to Nani's house. Her hands shake more now when she pours tea. I did her grocery list, paid her electricity bill on my phone and fixed the TV remote. She kept saying "you've grown up so much." I pretended it was nothing but honestly my throat got tight.

Being an adult is a lot of small boring things. But today they felt like they mattered.

Pallavi

qa.q: Who sat with Pallavi on the video call?
qa.a: Mehak.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi's throat get tight at Nani's house?
qa.a: Seeing her grandmother's shaking hands and hearing her say she'd grown up moved her, mixing love with a sense of how things are changing.

qa.q: What small habit could help Pallavi keep up both kinds of duty?
qa.a: Setting a regular weekly visit to Nani and keeping a folder of her own tax papers, so neither slips.

qa.q: How might Nani feel having her granddaughter help with bills and chores?
qa.a: She probably feels cared for and proud, as her comments show. 🤍

grounding: A young woman's diary records her first tax filing and caring tasks for her grandmother.

passage: In the village near Dharwad, the gram sabha met under the neem tree every second Sunday. Kavitha, twenty-one, came home every weekend now that her father's eyesight had grown weak; she read his letters to him, sorted his pension papers and walked him to the temple in the evenings. This Sunday she brought him to the meeting too, holding his elbow over the uneven ground. When the talk turned to the broken handpump near the school, most of the young people stayed at the edges, scrolling. Kavitha stood up and read out the complaint her father had dictated to her, plus her own count of how many children fetched water from far away. Her neighbour Sarika, who had come only to watch, stepped forward. 'I'll collect signatures from our lane.' Her father squeezed Kavitha's hand, hard.

qa.q: Where did the gram sabha meet?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: What does her father squeezing Kavitha's hand hard suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud and moved that she was speaking up and carrying his concern.

qa.q: How could Kavitha keep balancing care for her father with community work?
qa.a: She can keep involving him, as she did at the meeting, and share tasks with neighbours like Sarika so she isn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Sarika's view of the meeting have changed?
qa.a: She came only to watch, but seeing Kavitha speak made her want to take part herself.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult caring for an ageing parent while taking an active part in village welfare.

passage:
The municipal election in Copenhagen fell on a grey Tuesday, and Mei had circled it on her calendar in red. Nineteen, first vote. But her grandfather Emil had called that morning: his eyes were worse, and he wasn't sure he could read the ballot or manage the steps at the school.
Mei left her lecture early, took two buses to his flat and found him sitting in his coat, ready but anxious. “I've voted in every election since 1968,” he said. “I'm not stopping now.”
At the polling station she asked a volunteer about help for voters with poor sight. A magnifier sheet appeared. Emil read slowly, marked his choice, and folded the paper himself.
Then it was Mei's turn. Her hand shook a little. Emil stood behind the line and waited, as proud as if he'd voted twice.

qa.q: Where was the polling station?
qa.a: The polling station was at the school.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling while he sat in his coat that morning?
qa.a: He felt anxious about his eyes and the steps, but also determined not to miss an election.

qa.q: Which of Mei's actions helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking the volunteer about help for voters with poor sight mattered most, because it let Emil vote on his own.

qa.q: What would change if Mei had gone to vote alone that day?
qa.a: Emil might have missed an election for the first time since 1968, and Mei's first vote would have lost the pride they shared that morning.

grounding: A young woman honours her grandfather's independence while casting her own first vote.

The community centre in Nagpur smelled of antiseptic and tea on the morning of the blood donation camp. Sumit, twenty-one, had signed up to volunteer weeks ago. What he hadn't told anyone was that he'd brought his father.
Manoj had retired from driving buses in March. Since then he'd sat by the window most days, the newspaper folded unread.
“Papa, can you handle the register? You know how to talk to people.”
Manoj frowned, then took the pen. By ten he was calling donors by name, telling a nervous college student about his own first donation in 1990, sending people to the juice table with a joke.
At lunch Sumit watched him laugh with the camp doctor. On the bus home Manoj said, “Next camp, tell me the date first. I'll iron a shirt.”

qa.q: What job did Sumit ask his father to handle?
qa.a: He asked him to handle the register at the blood donation camp.

qa.q: What does Manoj's unread newspaper suggest about how he had been feeling since retiring?
qa.a: It suggests he felt low and restless, without a role to fill his days.

qa.q: What could Sumit do next to build on this?
qa.a: He could share the next camp's date early, as his father asked, and look for other volunteer work they could do together.

qa.q: How might the nervous college student have experienced Manoj at the register?
qa.a: The student likely felt calmer, hearing a friendly older man talk about his own first donation.

grounding: A young man includes his retired father in community welfare work, honouring him and serving others.

To: Ms Gargi Rao, Ward Officer, Ward 14 Subject: Broken streetlights on Masjid Lane
Dear Ms Rao,
I am a resident of 22 Masjid Lane and a first-time voter in our ward. For five weeks, three streetlights between the bakery and the clinic have been dark. I walk my Nani to the clinic every Thursday evening. Last week she tripped on the broken kerb in the dark and scraped both hands. She was lucky.
I have filed a complaint on the city helpline twice (numbers 4471 and 4502) and received no reply. I have also spoken to eleven neighbours, and they have signed the attached sheet.
Could you let me know when the lights and kerb will be repaired? I am happy to walk the lane with anyone from your office.
Thank you for your time.
Nazia Qureshi

qa.a: Eleven neighbours signed the attached sheet.

qa.q: How can you tell Nazia was worried after her Nani tripped?
qa.a: Nazia writes that Nani was lucky, which shows how shaken and concerned Nazia was about what could have happened.

qa.q: What makes Nazia's letter likely to be taken seriously?
qa.a: It is polite and specific, gives complaint numbers and neighbours' signatures, and offers to walk the lane with the office.

passage: I'm Hafsa, and I live across the courtyard from Anirban's family in Siliguri. He's twenty-two. His father had a stroke last winter. Since then, I've watched Anirban rearrange his whole life. He wakes early to help his father walk to the gate and back, every day. He moved his job to work from home. In the evenings, he's out with a clipboard; he started the lane's garbage-sorting drive and even got the municipal office to put new bins. July: Dolma, twenty-one, got her first salary slip and a reminder about filing her tax return. She ignored it. She also kept postponing visits to her mother in Kalimpong, three hours away.
August: Her cousin Irfan, a chartered accountant, visited. "You know there's a penalty if you miss the deadline?" He sat with her for an hour and showed her the official website. She filed it herself, with his help, feeling oddly grown-up.
October: Dolma took the bus to Kalimpong every other Sunday. She brought her mother's medicines and fixed the leaking tap. When floods hit the next district, she spent two weekends sorting relief supplies at the community hall. "Busy girl," her mother said, smiling. "Useful girl," Dolma replied.

qa.a: In Kalimpong, three hours away.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel after filing the tax return?
qa.a: She felt oddly grown-up and capable.

qa.q: What helped Dolma start meeting her duties?
qa.a: Irfan's help with the tax filing, then regular visits to her mother and volunteering for flood relief.

Avni, you ask why I make such a fuss about you voting. Let me tell you.
When I was twenty-one, I didn't bother. It was raining, I had a class, one vote didn't matter. My father went to the booth with his walking stick and came back soaked. He said nothing, but he looked at me, his only daughter.
That same year he fell ill, and I became the one who took him to the hospital, filed his papers and paid our house tax on time, because nobody else would.
Sitting in that government office, I understood: everything we have runs because people turn up and do the dull things.
The next election, I, Ankita, stood in the rain and voted. I took him too, in a wheelchair.
So go, beta. Your vote is not dull.

qa.q: What did Ankita's father use to walk to the booth?
qa.a: His walking stick.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when her father looked at her after voting?
qa.a: She likely felt ashamed and uneasy, knowing she had skipped voting while he went in the rain.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Ankita's story?
qa.a: Caring for her ill father and handling the family's taxes and papers, which made her understand civic duty.

qa.q: How might the father have felt being taken to vote in a wheelchair?
qa.a: He may have felt proud and moved that his daughter had taken up the duty.

grounding: An elder recalls learning civic duty and care for an ageing parent as a young adult.

passage:
On election day, the booth was two kilometres away, and the rain came down in sheets. Rukmini had her first vote and a grandmother who refused to miss hers.
The autos were full. Her cousin Ankita's scooter wouldn't start.
Rukmini borrowed a neighbour's big umbrella, wrapped her grandmother in a shawl, and walked her slowly, stopping under shop awnings. It took forty minutes.
At the booth, a volunteer found a chair for her grandmother in the queue. Rukmini's feet were soaked.
When they came out, ink on both their fingers, her grandmother said, "Your grandfather and I never missed one."
Rukmini laughed and squeezed her hand. On the way home, she thought about the papers for her grandmother's pension, due next week. She'd do them on Sunday.

qa.q: How long did the walk to the booth take?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel coming out of the booth?
qa.a: She felt proud and warm, laughing and squeezing her grandmother's hand.

qa.q: How did Rukmini manage the difficult conditions?
qa.a: She found a way on foot with an umbrella and a shawl, walking slowly and resting under awnings, instead of giving up.

qa.q: How might her grandmother see Rukmini's effort?
qa.a: Her grandmother likely feels touched and proud, reminded of her own years of voting.

grounding: Shows a young adult carrying out civic duty and caring for an elder despite obstacles.

Sarita had just started her first job when her landlord's notice came: the building was collecting signatures to fix the broken drain that flooded the lane every monsoon.
Most tenants ignored it. Sarita read it twice. She went door to door on Sunday with her neighbour Vijay, collecting signatures and explaining the complaint process at the ward office.
That evening her mother called from Nagpur. "You sound tired."
"Busy, Aai. Drain petition. Also I sent your medicine refill and filed my first tax return."
Her mother went quiet. "When did you become so grown-up?"
Sarita laughed. "Last week, I think."
A month later, workers came to fix the drain. Vijay grinned at her across the lane.

qa.q: What did the building want to fix?
qa.a: The broken drain that flooded the lane every monsoon.

qa.q: How did Sarita's mother seem to feel on the phone?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and touched, going quiet and then asking when Sarita became so grown-up.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that showed civic and family responsibility?
qa.a: She organised signatures for the drain, filed her tax return and sent her mother's medicine refill.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel when the drain gets fixed?
qa.a: Vijay likely feels proud and pleased, sharing credit for their Sunday effort.

grounding: Shows a young adult fulfilling civic, legal and family duties at once.

"Nani, your slip is in my bag. Ready?"
"Minakshi, I've voted in every election since before your mother was born. Of course I'm ready." Nani pulled her dupatta over her head. "Only my knees are not."
Pema, Minakshi's friend from college, looked up from the sofa. "Should I call an auto?"
"Already booked," Minakshi said. "I checked, the booth has a ramp, and elderly voters can go first."
Nani smiled. "And you? Your first time."
"My first time." Minakshi laughed nervously. "I read about all the candidates last night. I don't want to press the button just because someone told me to."
Pema said, "My parents said voting doesn't change anything."
Nani tapped the table. "My father walked six kilometres to vote. It changed him, at least."
At the booth, Minakshi held Nani's elbow up the ramp, then stood in her own line, staring at the ink mark on her finger after.

qa.q: How far did Nani's father walk to vote?
qa.a: He walked six kilometres to vote.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling about voting for the first time?
qa.a: She felt nervous but also proud and serious about it, which is why she read about the candidates instead of voting just because someone told her to.

qa.q: How could Pema respond to her parents' doubt about voting?
qa.a: Pema could share what she saw today, a first-time voter who studied the candidates and a grandmother who never missed an election, and talk it over with them.

qa.q: What is it like for Nani to go to the booth with Minakshi?
qa.a: Nani likely feels respected and cared for, since her granddaughter planned the auto, the ramp and the queue, and she gets to pass on a family habit.
